steps.body: One number, many splits. 6 breaks into 5 and 1, or 4 and 2, or 3 and 3.

6 is the whole — the other PART is 2.
4 and 3 make 7 — one too many. It is 2.

widget.missFeedback: The locked dots are the box of 4 — add just enough to show the whole 6.

explanationVariants: Start with 5 and 2. Moving one from the first part to the second makes 4 and 3, and 4 + 3 is still 7.
One part loses one while the other gains one, so the whole stays 7: 4 and 3.

widget.prompt: Seven is split into 5 and 2. Move one counter from the 5-part to the 2-part. Which new split do you get?

options.label: 5 and 3
options.feedback: That adds a counter instead of moving one. The first part must drop from 5 to 4.

options.label: 4 and 2
options.feedback: That removes a counter. The second part must grow from 2 to 3.

options.label: 4 and 3
options.feedback: Yes — 5 loses one and 2 gains one. The new split is 4 and 3, still making 7.

options.label: 6 and 1
options.feedback: That moves a counter in the opposite direction. From the 5-part to the 2-part gives 4 and 3.

hints: The first part loses one: 5 becomes 4.
The second part gains that same one: 2 becomes 3.
Check the whole: 4 and 3 still make 7.

steps.body: Numbers break into parts many ways. Parts joined make the whole again.
takeaways: A number splits into pairs of parts: 5 is 2 and 3, or 1 and 4.
Equal splits share evenly: 6 is 3 and 3.
Adding, taking away, splitting — you can do it all to 10!
steps.teaser: One big idea is left — how to MAKE TEN!

concept.body: Six can break into two parts in more than one way: **5 and 1**, **4 and 2**, or **3 and 3**. Each pair makes 6.
concept.narration: Six can break into two parts in more than one way: **5 and 1**, **4 and 2**, or **3 and 3**. Each pair makes 6.

widget.prompt: 5 candies split between two hands. One hand has 2. How many in the other?

options.feedback: 5 is the whole — the other hand holds 3.
2 and 2 make only 4 — the other hand holds 3.
2 and 4 make 6 — one too many. It is 3.
